claims.text: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is ductile.
As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 has an FCC/BCC dual-phase microstructure.
The as-cast alloy has a random atomic distribution and no significant L12/B2 ordering.
Aging AlCoCrFeNi2.1 at approximately 600°C induces a brittle state.
Aging AlCoCrFeNi2.1 at approximately 750°C restores ductility.
Chemical ordering is maximal in the 600°C aging regime.
Aging temperature can alter chemical ordering in Al-containing Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys.
The relevant microstructure contains jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries.
Nanometer-scale L12/B2 ordered domains form within the FCC matrix.
At 600°C, ordered domains approach a stoichiometric Ni3Al-like composition.
Near-stoichiometric Ni3Al-like ordering raises the antiphase boundary energy.
Chemical ordering affects mechanical behavior in compositionally complex FCC alloys.
High antiphase boundary energy restricts dislocation cross-slip and promotes planar slip.
Planar slip produces stress concentration at serrations of jagged phase boundaries and thereby causes brittle fracture.
At 750°C, the order parameter and antiphase boundary energy decrease, restoring cross-slip.
Antiphase boundary energy peaks and elongation reaches a minimum at 600°C.
The brittle state exhibits planar slip traces terminating at jagged boundaries, whereas the ductile state exhibits wavy slip and cross-slip.
The transition occurs when the SRO/LRO degree raises APBE above a critical condition for cross-slip.
APBE can be estimated from dislocation dissociation widths observed by HRTEM.
Superlattice-reflection intensities can be used to quantify the degree of chemical ordering.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis repeatedly treats L12 and B2 as a single type of ordered domain and describes Ni3Al-like domains as 'L12/B2.' L12 and B2 are distinct ordered crystal structures, while near-stoichiometric Ni3Al conventionally identifies L12 ordering; the proposed phase identity is therefore internally ambiguous.
